text: More than 2,500 years ago, the Celtic peoples lived across much of Europe, from Ireland and Britain to southern Germany.
Their holy places included round sites in Ireland, such as the Hill of Tara.
src: date to the 6th and 5th centuries BCE / The Celtic peoples practised their religion across much of Iron Age Europe, from Ireland and Britain through Gaul and Belgica to southern Germany
circular sites in Ireland, of which the Hill of Tara and Navan Fort are the most notable

text: The Celts believed in many gods, and the names of over two hundred still survive.
Lugus was a god of skill and craft, and Epona was the goddess of horses.
src: Celtic religion was polytheistic. Over two hundred names of deities survive
Lugus a god of skill and craft / Epona, goddess of horses

text: Their priests were called druids, and people gave gifts to the gods in sacred groves and at springs.
They threw weapons and treasures into rivers, lakes and bogs as offerings.
src: Its priests were the druids / Offerings were made throughout the landscape: in sacred groves called nemeta, at springs and in timber temples
Weapons and treasures were thrown into rivers, lakes and bogs

text: The Celts wrote nothing down about their religion.
Much later, Christian monks wrote down Irish and Welsh tales, where the old gods became heroes with special powers.
src: the Celts wrote nothing down about their religion
The Irish and Welsh tales were written down by Christian monks / In them the gods become heroes with supernatural powers

text: Slowly the Celtic peoples became Christians, and the old religion died out.
Yet some old customs live on, like the festival of Beltane and visits to holy wells.
src: it died out as the Celtic peoples converted to Christianity
Beltane is still kept / pilgrimages to holy wells
